```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(PKNCA)
simulation <- readRDS("v24-sparse-auc-to-infinity-simulation.rds")
mean_type <- readRDS("v24-sparse-auc-to-infinity-mean-type.rds")
bootstrap <- readRDS("v24-sparse-auc-to-infinity-bootstrap.rds")
bootstrap_n <- readRDS("v24-sparse-auc-to-infinity-bootstrap-n.rds")
tobit <- readRDS("v24-sparse-auc-to-infinity-tobit.rds")
tobit$summary <-
  merge(
    tobit$summary,
    tobit$scenarios[, c("scenario", "compartments", "route", "design", "blq", "elimination")],
    by = "scenario"
  )
# The rows of a simulation summary that match every given column value
sim_rows <- function(summary, filters) {
  keep <- rep(TRUE, nrow(summary))
  for (current_name in names(filters)) {
    keep <- keep & summary[[current_name]] %in% filters[[current_name]]
  }
  summary[keep, ]
}
# The range of a column of the standard error study over the rows matching
# `...` (column = value), as text
se_range <- function(column, ..., digits = 0) {
  v <- sim_rows(simulation$summary, list(...))[[column]]
  paste(format(round(range(v), digits), nsmall = digits), collapse = " to ")
}
# The same for the bootstrap study
boot_range <- function(column, ..., digits = 0) {
  v <- sim_rows(bootstrap$summary, list(...))[[column]]
  paste(format(round(range(v), digits), nsmall = digits), collapse = " to ")
}
# One value of the profile over the number of animals per time
profile_value <- function(column, n_per_time, blq, method, parameter, digits = 1) {
  v <- sim_rows(bootstrap_n$summary, list(n_per_time = n_per_time, blq = blq, method = method, parameter = parameter))[[column]]
  stopifnot(length(v) == 1)
  format(round(v, digits), nsmall = digits)
}
# The same for the Tobit half-life study
tobit_range <- function(column, ..., digits = 0) {
  v <- sim_rows(tobit$summary, list(...))[[column]]
  paste(format(round(range(v), digits), nsmall = digits), collapse = " to ")
}
tobit_value <- function(column, ..., digits = 1) {
  v <- sim_rows(tobit$summary, list(...))[[column]]
  stopifnot(length(v) == 1)
  format(round(v, digits), nsmall = digits)
}
# The same for the arithmetic and geometric mean profile study
mt_range <- function(column, ..., digits = 0) {
  v <- sim_rows(mean_type$summary, list(...))[[column]]
  paste(format(round(range(v), digits), nsmall = digits), collapse = " to ")
}
# The comparisons with published methods (PK package, Wolfsegger and Jaki
# 2005, and PKNCA's bootstrap-t) and with the BLOQ package's BLQ treatments
comparisons <- readRDS("v24-sparse-auc-to-infinity-comparisons.rds")
blq <- readRDS("v24-sparse-auc-to-infinity-blq.rds")
# The range, or the one value, of a column of any summary over the rows
# matching `...` (column = value), as text
summary_range <- function(summary, column, ..., digits = 0) {
  v <- sim_rows(summary, list(...))[[column]]
  stopifnot(length(v) > 0)
  paste(unique(format(round(range(v), digits), nsmall = digits)), collapse = " to ")
}
summary_value <- function(summary, column, ..., digits = 1) {
  v <- sim_rows(summary, list(...))[[column]]
  stopifnot(length(v) == 1)
  format(round(v, digits), nsmall = digits)
}
cmp_range <- function(column, ..., digits = 0) summary_range(comparisons$summary, column, ..., digits = digits)
blq_range <- function(column, ..., digits = 0) summary_range(blq$summary, column, ..., digits = digits)
# The AUC to infinity in the serial-sacrifice comparisons
serial_range <- function(column, interval, n_per_time, ..., digits = 1) {
  cmp_range(column, interval = interval, design = "serial", parameter = "auc", n_per_time = n_per_time, ..., digits = digits)
}
# The batch-design comparisons
batch_range <- function(column, interval, parameter, ..., digits = 1) {
  cmp_range(column, interval = interval, design = "batch", parameter = parameter, ..., digits = digits)
}
# The percentage of data sets whose interval could not be calculated, from
# the number of data sets of each cell
failure_range <- function(..., digits = 1) {
  r <- sim_rows(comparisons$summary, list(...))
  v <- 100*(1 - r$n/comparisons$n_replicates)
  paste(unique(format(round(range(v), digits), nsmall = digits)), collapse = " to ")
}
# The largest drop in coverage (percentage points) from counting a failure as
# a miss
max_coverage_drop <- function(..., digits = 1) {
  r <- sim_rows(comparisons$summary, list(...))
  format(round(max(r$coverage*(1 - r$n/comparisons$n_replicates)), digits), nsmall = digits)
}
# The bias (%) of an estimator with many animals per time
large_range <- function(estimator, ..., digits = 1) {
  summary_range(comparisons$large_n_summary, "relative_bias", estimator = estimator, ..., digits = digits)
}
# The ratio of the median widths of PKNCA's bootstrap-t and delta-method
# intervals over the number of animals per time
boott_width_ratio <- function(n_per_time, blq, parameter, digits = 2) {
  rows <- list(n_per_time = n_per_time, blq = blq, parameter = parameter)
  boot_t <- sim_rows(comparisons$profile_summary, c(rows, list(interval = "pknca boot-t")))$median_ci_width
  delta <- sim_rows(comparisons$profile_summary, c(rows, list(interval = "pknca delta")))$median_ci_width
  stopifnot(length(boot_t) == 1, length(delta) == 1)
  format(round(boot_t/delta, digits), nsmall = digits)
}
# PKNCA's intervals over the number of animals per time
boott_value <- function(column, n_per_time, blq, parameter, interval = "pknca boot-t", digits = 1) {
  summary_value(
    comparisons$profile_summary, column,
    interval = interval, n_per_time = n_per_time, blq = blq, parameter = parameter, digits = digits
  )
}
```

# Summary and recommendations

For sparse sampling, where each animal gives one or a few samples:

* **Use the delta-method standard error for the AUC to infinity (the
  default).**  When little of the AUC is extrapolated, Yuan's standard error,
  which treats $\lambda_z$ as known, and the delta method both cover close to
  the nominal 95% (Yuan `r se_range("coverage", method = "yuan", parameter = "auc", elimination = "fast")`%).
  When about a fifth of the AUC is extrapolated, Yuan's intervals are too
  narrow (`r se_range("coverage", method = "yuan", parameter = "auc", elimination = "slow")`%
  coverage), and the delta method is closer to nominal
  (`r se_range("coverage", method = "delta", parameter = "auc", elimination = "slow")`%).
  Set `sparse_lambda_z_se = "none"` for Yuan's method.
* **Give the AUC a concentration at time 0.**  As for any PKNCA AUC, the sparse
  AUC is `NA` without one.  Sacrificial designs rarely sample at the dose, so
  after an extravascular dose impute zero with `impute = "start_conc0"`.  After
  an IV bolus, request the IV parameters (`aucivlast`, `aucivinf.obs`):  they
  back-extrapolate $C_0$ from the mean profile and include its uncertainty.
* **Treat the AUMC, and the MRT and Vss that come from it, with caution.**  The
  AUMC to infinity was biased low in most scenarios, and its confidence intervals
  under-covered in every scenario, even with the delta method
  (`r se_range("coverage", method = "delta", parameter = "aumc")`%), most when
  elimination was slow.  PKNCA gives no standard error for the MRT or $V_{ss}$;
  the PK package's intervals for them under-covered in the batch design
  (`r batch_range("coverage", "pk z", "mrt", blq = "none")`% for the MRT),
  as its help warns, because the MRT of the mean profile is itself biased.
* **The half-life of the mean profile is not the typical animal's half-life.**
  It was too long when the terminal phase was well sampled (by up to
  `r max(round(sim_rows(mean_type$summary, list(mean_type = "arithmetic", parameter = "half.life", elimination = "fast", blq = "none"))$bias_typical))`%)
  and too short when the profile was cut short by BLQ samples or a two-compartment
  distribution (down to
  `r min(round(sim_rows(mean_type$summary, list(mean_type = "arithmetic", parameter = "half.life"))$bias_typical))`%).
  Sample long enough to see at least three terminal half-lives.
* **Cmax of the mean profile reads high with few animals per time.**  Taking
  the maximum of noisy means near a broad peak overestimated Cmax by up to
  `r max(round(sim_rows(mean_type$summary, list(mean_type = "arithmetic", parameter = "cmax", route = "oral"))$bias_natural))`%.
* **Geometric-mean profiles were evaluated and not adopted.**  They were no more
  biased and were as precise or modestly more precise, but they estimate a
  different quantity (the typical animal rather than the population mean
  curve), need a rule for BLQ samples that drives their BLQ results, and fall
  outside the variance methods for sparse AUCs, which are for arithmetic means;
  adopting them would change all sparse calculations for a modest gain.
* **The bootstrap (`sparse_bootstrap()`) gives intervals for any parameter, but
  they are too narrow with few animals at each time.**  With three or four
  animals per time, its 95% intervals for the AUC to infinity covered
  `r boot_range("coverage_percentile", parameter = "auc")`% of the time.  Prefer
  the analytical standard errors for the AUCs, and use the bootstrap for
  parameters and comparisons that have none, such as Cmax and ratios between
  groups.  With 20 or more animals per time, its standard error was accurate
  and its intervals matched the delta method's.  A bootstrap-$t$ on the
  delta-method standard error covered the AUMC better than the delta method,
  but not the AUC, and it was not adopted:  it keeps the same, biased
  estimate, and its gain comes from a wider or shifted interval around it.
* **With many animals, the bias of the sparse estimate dominates.**  BLQ
  samples and the extrapolation of the mean profile biased the AUC to infinity
  low (by about
  `r gsub("-", "", profile_value("median_bias", 100, "moderate", "yuan", "auc", digits = 0))`%
  with BLQ samples here), whatever the number of animals and whichever
  half-life was used, so with many animals every confidence interval missed the
  truth more often than its nominal level.
* **The published intervals for these designs did not cover better with few
  animals.**  With three animals per time in serial-sacrifice designs, the delta
  method covered `r serial_range("coverage", "pknca delta", 3)`%.  The
  bootstrap-$t$ of Wolfsegger and Jaki (2005) covered about as well without
  BLQ samples, but with intervals about twice as wide from an unstable estimate.
  Both it and the PK package take the logarithm of every sample, and they broke
  down with BLQ samples:  with slow elimination, PK's asymptotic interval
  covered
  `r serial_range("coverage", "pk z", 3, blq = "moderate", elimination = "slow", digits = 0)`%
  and the 2005 bootstrap-$t$
  `r serial_range("coverage", "wj2005 boot-t", 3, blq = "moderate", elimination = "slow", digits = 0)`%.
* **Imputing BLQ samples was evaluated and not adopted.**  The treatments that
  Barnett et al. (2021) compared, applied at each time, reduced the bias of the
  AUC to infinity with slow elimination (kernel imputation
  `r blq_range("median_bias", elimination = "slow", interval = "kernel delta", digits = 1)`%,
  against
  `r blq_range("median_bias", elimination = "slow", interval = "zero delta", digits = 1)`%
  for zero), but none covered better than zero substitution, and the direct
  censored likelihood under-covered.
* **The Tobit half-life was evaluated with BLQ samples and not adopted for the
  sparse AUC.**  The Tobit fit of the mean profile (`hl_method = "tobit"`, with
  the LLOQ carried through the mean profile) gave nearly the same AUC to
  infinity as the log-linear fit, and it has no delta-method standard error.  A
  (mixed-effects) Tobit fit of the individual samples was slightly less biased
  and more precise, but its standard error added to Yuan's covered less well
  than the delta method with slow elimination
  (`r tobit_range("coverage", interval = "tobit-individual yuan+var", parameter = "auc", elimination = "slow", n_per_time = 4)`%
  against `r tobit_range("coverage", interval = "log-linear delta", parameter = "auc", elimination = "slow", n_per_time = 4)`%),
  and neither Tobit fit removed the bias that BLQ samples cause.

# Introduction

With sparse sampling, each animal contributes only one or a few samples to a
concentration-time profile, so there is no individual AUC to summarize.
Instead, the AUC is estimated from the mean concentration at each time, and its
standard error comes from the variability between animals at each time.  Bailer
(1988) gave the estimator and its variance for the AUC from time 0 to the last
sampling time with serial sacrifice (one sample per animal).  Nedelman and Jia
(1998) extended it to designs where animals give more than one sample, with
a Satterthwaite approximation for the degrees of freedom, and Holder (2001)
gave an unbiased estimator of the covariance between times.  Yuan (1993)
extended Bailer's method to the AUC from 0 to infinity by adding the
extrapolation $\bar{y}_n/\lambda_z$, treating the terminal elimination rate
$\lambda_z$ as known.

Wolfsegger and Jaki (2005) estimated the AUC to infinity in serial sacrifice
designs with $\lambda_z$ fit to the mean concentrations of the time points after
the last one in the trapezoidal sum, so that the two parts of the estimate are
independent by construction, and built bootstrap-$t$ intervals on the resulting
variance; they noted that using the covariance between the trapezoidal AUC and
$\lambda_z$, so that the same samples serve both, was a subject for further
research.  Jaki and Wolfsegger (2009) gave one estimator and variance of the
AUC to the last time for complete, batch, and serial sacrifice designs, and Jaki
and Wolfsegger (2012) extended the serial-sampling parameters of Wolfsegger and
Jaki (2009), the AUC and AUMC to infinity, MRT, half-life, clearance, and
$V_{ss}$ after an IV bolus, to those designs, with asymptotic and bootstrap-$t$
intervals, as implemented in the R package PK (Jaki and Wolfsegger 2011).  Barnett, Geys, Jacobs, and Jaki
(2021) compared eight treatments of samples below the limit of quantification
in the AUC, from substitution to censored maximum likelihood and kernel-density
imputation.

In practice, $\lambda_z$ is estimated from the same data, so its uncertainty
adds to that of the AUC to infinity.  This vignette describes how PKNCA
calculates the sparse AUC and AUMC to infinity with their standard errors and
degrees of freedom, gives a delta-method extension of Yuan's method that
includes the uncertainty in $\lambda_z$ and its covariance with the means (the
covariance Wolfsegger and Jaki left open), extends both to IV bolus dosing, and
compares the methods in a simulation-estimation study, with the estimators of
Wolfsegger and Jaki (2005) and of the PK package, a bootstrap-$t$ interval, and
the treatments of BLQ samples that Barnett et al. (2021) compared.  A second
study compares arithmetic and geometric mean profiles.

# The sparse AUC to the last measurement

At each sampling time $t_i$ ($i = 0, \ldots, n$), $r_i$ animals are sampled and
$\bar{y}_i$ is the arithmetic mean concentration.  $r_{ij}$ animals are sampled
at both $t_i$ and $t_j$ ($r_{ii} = r_i$).  The linear trapezoidal AUC of the
mean profile is a weighted sum of the means,

$$\widehat{AUC}_{0-t_{last}} = \sum_{i=0}^{n} w_i \bar{y}_i,
\quad w_0 = \frac{t_1 - t_0}{2},
\quad w_i = \frac{t_{i+1} - t_{i-1}}{2},
\quad w_n = \frac{t_n - t_{n-1}}{2},$$

where $t_n = t_{last}$ is the last time with a positive mean.  Since the
estimate is linear in the means, its variance is

$$\text{Var}\left(\widehat{AUC}_{0-t_{last}}\right) = \sum_{i}\sum_{j} w_i w_j \frac{r_{ij}\,\sigma_{ij}}{r_i r_j},$$

with $\sigma_{ij}$ the covariance of the concentrations at $t_i$ and $t_j$
within an animal.  PKNCA estimates $\sigma_{ii}$ with the sample variance and
$\sigma_{ij}$ ($i \neq j$) with the unbiased estimator of Holder (2001), setting
it to 0 when fewer than two animals are sampled at both times.  With serial
sacrifice, $r_{ij} = 0$ for $i \neq j$ and this is Bailer's (1988) variance,
$\sum_i w_i^2 s_i^2/r_i$.

Only times up to $t_{last}$ have weight.  When more than half of the samples at
a time are below the limit of quantification (BLQ), PKNCA sets that time's mean
to zero; times after the last positive mean are not part of
$AUC_{0-t_{last}}$, and they contribute nothing to its variance either.

As for any AUC in PKNCA, the area starts at the start of the interval, so a
concentration is needed there, measured or imputed; without one, the sparse
AUC is `NA`.  Animals are rarely sampled at the dose in sacrificial designs, so
after an extravascular dose the usual choice is to impute a concentration of
zero with `impute = "start_conc0"`.  An imputed zero is known rather than
measured, so it has weight in the estimate (as $\bar{y}_0 = 0$) but no
variance.

# Extrapolation to infinity (Yuan 1993)

With first-order terminal elimination, the area after $t_{last}$ is
$\bar{y}_{n}/\lambda_z$, so

$$\widehat{AUC}_{0-\infty} = \sum_{i=0}^{n} w_i \bar{y}_i + \frac{\bar{y}_n}{\lambda_z}.$$

This is still linear in the means if $\lambda_z$ is known, with the last weight
increased by $1/\lambda_z$.  Yuan's (1993) variance (his equation 4) is
Bailer's with that weight, $g_n = w_n + 1/\lambda_z$:

$$\text{Var}\left(\widehat{AUC}_{0-\infty}\right) = \sum_{i}\sum_{j} g_i g_j \frac{r_{ij}\,\sigma_{ij}}{r_i r_j},
\qquad g_i = w_i + \frac{\delta_{i,n}}{\lambda_z}.$$

Written this way, the method applies to any sampling design, not only serial
sacrifice.

The AUMC is the AUC of the moment curve $t\,C(t)$.  Its estimate uses the
moment means $\bar{m}_i = t_i \bar{y}_i$, and the extrapolation
$t_{last} C_{last}/\lambda_z + C_{last}/\lambda_z^2$ is
$\bar{m}_n\left(1/\lambda_z + 1/(t_{last}\lambda_z^2)\right)$, so the AUMC
weights are $g_i = w_i + \delta_{i,n}\left(1/\lambda_z + 1/(t_{last}\lambda_z^2)\right)$
applied to the moment means, with the covariances of the moments
$t_i t_j \sigma_{ij}$.

# IV bolus:  the back-extrapolated C0

After an IV bolus, the concentration at time 0 is not zero, and it cannot be
measured.  As for dense data, PKNCA estimates it from the mean profile with the
methods of `pk.calc.c0()`:  log-linear back-extrapolation from the first two
means when they decline,

$$\hat{C}_0 = \bar{y}_1 \left(\frac{\bar{y}_1}{\bar{y}_2}\right)^{t_1/(t_2 - t_1)},$$

and otherwise $\bar{y}_1$.  The AUC adds the trapezoid from time 0 to $t_1$,
$t_1(\hat{C}_0 + \bar{y}_1)/2$.  $\hat{C}_0$ is a smooth function of the
first two means, so its uncertainty enters the variance through its gradient,
as in the next section:  the weights of $\bar{y}_1$ and $\bar{y}_2$ gain
$(t_1/2)\,\partial \hat{C}_0/\partial \bar{y}_j$, with

$$\frac{\partial \hat{C}_0}{\partial \bar{y}_1} = \frac{\hat{C}_0\, t_2}{(t_2 - t_1)\,\bar{y}_1},
\qquad
\frac{\partial \hat{C}_0}{\partial \bar{y}_2} = -\frac{\hat{C}_0\, t_1}{(t_2 - t_1)\,\bar{y}_2}.$$

With the linear trapezoidal rule, the AUMC from time 0 to $t_1$ is
$t_1^2\bar{y}_1/2$ whatever $C_0$ is, so $C_0$ does not affect the AUMC.  These
are the sparse `aucivlast`, `aucivall`, and `aucivinf.obs` (and their AUMC
equivalents), each with its standard error and degrees of freedom.

# The uncertainty of lambda.z (delta method)

$\lambda_z$ is estimated from the mean profile:  PKNCA fits a line to the log
mean concentrations at the half-life points, chosen automatically by the
adjusted $r^2$ (see `vignette("v06-half-life-calculation")`).  For a given
set of half-life points $H$, the estimate is minus the least-squares slope,

$$\hat{\lambda}_z = -\sum_{j \in H} c_j \log \bar{y}_j,
\qquad c_j = \frac{t_j - \bar{t}_H}{\sum_{k \in H}\left(t_k - \bar{t}_H\right)^2},$$

a smooth function of the means.  So $\widehat{AUC}_{0-\infty}$ is a smooth
function of the means, and the delta method gives its variance from the same
covariance of the means with the gradient in place of the weights:

$$g_j = \frac{\partial \widehat{AUC}_{0-\infty}}{\partial \bar{y}_j}
= w_j + \frac{\delta_{j,n}}{\lambda_z}
+ \frac{\bar{y}_n}{\lambda_z^2}\,\frac{c_j}{\bar{y}_j}\,\mathbb{1}_{j \in H}.$$

The last term is the uncertainty in $\lambda_z$.  Because the gradient is taken
with respect to all of the means together, the variance includes the covariance
of $\hat{\lambda}_z$ with $\bar{y}_n$ and with $\widehat{AUC}_{0-t_{last}}$.
Those covariances matter:  a high mean at an early half-life point raises the
AUC to $t_{last}$ but steepens the slope, which lowers the extrapolated area,
so the two partly cancel.  Adding a separately estimated variance of
$\hat{\lambda}_z$ to Yuan's variance would miss that.

For the AUMC, with the moment means,
$\hat{\lambda}_z = -\sum_{j \in H} c_j \left(\log \bar{m}_j - \log t_j\right)$ and

$$g_j = w_j + \delta_{j,n}\left(\frac{1}{\lambda_z} + \frac{1}{t_{last}\lambda_z^2}\right)
+ \bar{m}_n\left(\frac{1}{\lambda_z^2} + \frac{2}{t_{last}\lambda_z^3}\right)\frac{c_j}{\bar{m}_j}\,\mathbb{1}_{j \in H}.$$

The method conditions on the selected half-life points:  the variability from
choosing them is not included.  It is a first-order approximation, which is
most accurate when the coefficient of variation of the means at the half-life
points is small.

# Degrees of freedom

Confidence intervals use a $t$ distribution.  The variance estimate is a
quadratic form in the individual measurements $y$, $\hat{V} = y^T M y$, where
$M$ centers the measurements at each time and weights the products of each
animal's measurements by $g_i g_j r_{ij}/(r_i r_j h_{ij})$, with $h_{ij}$ the
divisor of the Holder covariance.  With $\Omega$ the covariance of the
measurements, Nedelman and Jia's (1998) equation 6 gives the Satterthwaite
degrees of freedom,

$$\nu = \frac{2\,E^2}{V}, \qquad E = \text{tr}(M\Omega), \qquad V = 2\,\text{tr}(M\Omega M\Omega).$$

With serial sacrifice, this is equation 6a of Nedelman, Gibiansky, and Lau
(1995).  PKNCA uses the same expression with the weights $g$ for the AUC and
AUMC to infinity, with or without the delta-method terms.

# An alternative:  lambda.z from the individual samples

Instead of the log means, $\lambda_z$ could be estimated from every individual
sample in the terminal phase, with its standard error from that regression.
Samples below the limit of quantification are censored, so the regression is a
Tobit regression on the log concentrations; when animals give more than one
sample, a random intercept for each animal accounts for their correlation.  The
variance of $\hat{\lambda}_z$ is then added to Yuan's variance.

Two properties of this approach differ from the delta method.  A line through
the individual log concentrations follows the geometric-mean profile, while the
AUC and $C_{last}$ come from the arithmetic means; the two have the same
terminal slope only when the between-animal coefficient of variation is the
same at every terminal time.  And the regression does not give the covariance of
$\hat{\lambda}_z$ with the means, so it is added as though it were independent.
The simulation below compares both.

# Simulation-estimation study

```{r simulation-details, echo = FALSE}
model <- simulation$model
```

## Design

Every study in this vignette shares one design.  The simulations are a targets
pipeline in `data-raw/sparse-simulation/` of the PKNCA source; its README says
how to run it, how long it takes, and how to add a scenario or an estimator.
Concentrations come
from one- and two-compartment models (pmxTools) after a dose of
`r model$dose`, given orally or as an IV bolus, with log-normal between-animal
variability (`r 100*model$omega`% on each structural parameter) and a
multiplicative residual error (`r 100*model$sigma`%) with mean 1:

* **One compartment:**  $V$ `r simulation$model_1cmt$v`, $k_e$ 0.15/hr (fast
  elimination, half-life 4.6 hr) or 0.07/hr (slow, 9.9 hr), and oral $k_a$
  `r simulation$model_1cmt$ka`/hr (Tmax 0.7 to 0.9 hr).
* **Two compartments:**  $V_1$ `r simulation$model_2cmt$v1`, $V_2$
  `r simulation$model_2cmt$v2`, $Q$ `r simulation$model_2cmt$q`, and $CL$
  chosen for the same terminal half-lives after a distribution phase with a
  half-life of about 0.5 hr; oral $k_a$ `r simulation$model_2cmt$ka`/hr (Tmax
  0.6 to 0.7 hr).

The slow elimination leaves about a fifth of the AUC to extrapolate after 24
hours, and the fast elimination less than a tenth.  Two limits of
quantification gave no BLQ samples or about a third of the samples at 24 hours
BLQ (70% of the typical concentration at 24 hours).  No animal was sampled at
the dose.  The serial-sacrifice design sampled `r simulation$n_serial` animals
at each of `r length(simulation$sampling_times$oral)` times
(`r paste(signif(simulation$sampling_times$oral, 2), collapse = ", ")` hours
for oral dosing; for IV bolus dosing, the first time was 5 minutes and 6 hours
was omitted); the batch design sampled three batches of
`r simulation$n_batch` animals, each batch at a third of those times.  With
`r nrow(simulation$scenarios)` scenarios (two models, two routes, two designs,
two limits of quantification, and two elimination rates), the standard error
study had `r format(simulation$n_replicates, big.mark = ",")` replicates per
scenario.

The truth is the AUC (and AUMC) from 0 to infinity of the population mean
concentration curve, which is what the arithmetic means estimate:  the mean of
the individual values over `r format(simulation$n_virtual, big.mark = ",")`
virtual animals (Monte Carlo standard error at most
`r round(max(simulation$truth_mcse_percent[, c("auc", "aumc")]), 2)`%).  For
each replicate, the oral concentration at time 0 was imputed as zero and the IV
bolus $C_0$ was back-extrapolated, the half-life was fit to the mean profile as
PKNCA does, and three standard errors were calculated:

* **Yuan:**  $\lambda_z$ treated as known (`sparse_lambda_z_se = "none"`);
* **Delta:**  the delta method for $\lambda_z$ (`sparse_lambda_z_se = "delta"`);
* **Individual:**  $\lambda_z$ and its standard error from a Tobit regression
  of the individual samples from the first half-life time onward (with a random
  intercept for each animal in the batch design), with that $\lambda_z$ in the
  extrapolation and its variance added to Yuan's.

This study was run with PKNCA `r simulation$pknca_version` and pmxTools
`r simulation$pmxtools_version` (`r simulation$r_version`,
`r simulation$run_date`); every replicate has its own seed, so the results can
be reproduced.

```{r simulation-results, echo = FALSE}
results <- simulation$summary
scenario_columns <- function(r) {
  data.frame(
    Model = paste0(r$compartments, "-cmt"),
    Route = ifelse(r$route == "iv", "IV bolus", "oral"),
    Design = r$design,
    BLQ = r$blq,
    Elimination = r$elimination
  )
}
# One row per scenario with a column of `column` for each method
by_method <- function(parameter, column, methods, digits = 1) {
  r <- results[results$parameter == parameter, ]
  scenarios <- sort(unique(r$scenario))
  ret <- data.frame(scenario = scenarios)
  for (current_method in methods) {
    current <- r[r$method == current_method, ]
    ret[[current_method]] <- round(current[[column]][match(scenarios, current$scenario)], digits)
  }
  ret
}
show_coverage <- function(parameter) {
  r <- results[results$parameter == parameter & results$method == "yuan", ]
  r <- r[order(r$scenario), ]
  coverage <- by_method(parameter, "coverage", c("yuan", "delta", "individual"))
  width <- by_method(parameter, "median_ci_width", c("yuan", "delta", "individual"), digits = 0)
  out <-
    data.frame(
      scenario_columns(r),
      `Extrap. (%)` = round(r$percent_extrapolated, 1),
      `Coverage Yuan` = coverage$yuan,
      `Coverage delta` = coverage$delta,
      `Coverage indiv.` = coverage$individual,
      `CI width Yuan` = width$yuan,
      `CI width delta` = width$delta,
      `CI width indiv.` = width$individual,
      check.names = FALSE
    )
  knitr::kable(out, row.names = FALSE)
}
show_accuracy <- function(parameter) {
  r <- results[results$parameter == parameter & results$method == "yuan", ]
  r <- r[order(r$scenario), ]
  bias <- by_method(parameter, "relative_bias", c("yuan", "individual"))
  mae <- by_method(parameter, "median_absolute_error", c("yuan", "individual"))
  rmse <- by_method(parameter, "rmse", c("yuan", "individual"))
  out <-
    data.frame(
      scenario_columns(r),
      `Bias mean` = bias$yuan,
      `Bias indiv.` = bias$individual,
      `MAE mean` = mae$yuan,
      `MAE indiv.` = mae$individual,
      `RMSE mean` = rmse$yuan,
      `RMSE indiv.` = rmse$individual,
      check.names = FALSE
    )
  knitr::kable(out, row.names = FALSE)
}
```

## Results:  coverage of the AUC to infinity

```{r simulation-auc-coverage, echo = FALSE}
show_coverage("auc")
```

## Results:  coverage of the AUMC to infinity

```{r simulation-aumc-coverage, echo = FALSE}
show_coverage("aumc")
```

Coverage is the percentage of 95% confidence intervals that contain the truth,
and the CI width is the median width relative to the truth (%).  The Monte Carlo
standard error of each coverage is at most
`r round(max(simulation$summary$coverage_mcse), 1)` percentage points.

## Results:  the bootstrap

The bootstrap of Shen and Machado (2017) (`sparse_bootstrap()`) was run on the
first `r format(bootstrap$n_replicates, big.mark = ",")` data sets of each
scenario with `r bootstrap$n_boot` replicates each, its default.  Each replicate
resampled the animals within each sampling time (or batch), and its AUC and
AUMC to infinity were calculated as for the original data.  Two intervals were
formed:  the percentile interval of the replicates and the estimate plus or
minus 1.96 bootstrap standard errors (the standard deviation of the
replicates).  The delta method (on all of the scenario's data sets, which
include these) is shown for comparison.

```{r simulation-bootstrap, echo = FALSE}
show_bootstrap <- function(parameter) {
  b <- bootstrap$summary[bootstrap$summary$parameter == parameter, ]
  b <- b[order(b$scenario), ]
  delta <- results[results$parameter == parameter & results$method == "delta", ]
  delta <- delta[match(b$scenario, delta$scenario), ]
  out <-
    data.frame(
      scenario_columns(b),
      `Coverage percentile` = round(b$coverage_percentile, 1),
      `Coverage boot. SE` = round(b$coverage_normal, 1),
      `Coverage delta` = round(delta$coverage, 1),
      `CI width percentile` = round(b$median_ci_width_percentile),
      `CI width delta` = round(delta$median_ci_width),
      check.names = FALSE
    )
  knitr::kable(out, row.names = FALSE)
}
```

```{r simulation-bootstrap-auc, echo = FALSE}
show_bootstrap("auc")
```

```{r simulation-bootstrap-aumc, echo = FALSE}
show_bootstrap("aumc")
```

## Results:  the bootstrap with more animals at each time

Published uses of the bootstrap had either a few animals per time (three mice in
Takemoto et al. 2006, which compared only the means and standard deviations
with Bailer's) or many (about 88 subjects per time and treatment in the
bioequivalence study of Shen and Machado 2017), and Tardivon et al. (2023)
compared it with a model-based test for single-sample bioequivalence studies,
but not with an analytical standard error.  To see how the number of
animals per time changes the comparison, the two-compartment, oral,
serial-sacrifice design with slow elimination was simulated with
`r paste(bootstrap_n$n_per_time, collapse = ", ")` animals per time, without
and with BLQ samples (`r format(bootstrap_n$n_replicates, big.mark = ",")` data
sets each, `r bootstrap_n$n_boot` bootstrap replicates).  The data seeds do not depend on the
number of animals, so 4 animals per time reproduces the data sets above.  The
bias is that of the point estimate, which all of the methods share.

```{r simulation-bootstrap-n, echo = FALSE}
show_bootstrap_n <- function(parameter) {
  b <- bootstrap_n$summary[bootstrap_n$summary$parameter == parameter, ]
  keys <- unique(b[, c("blq", "n_per_time")])
  keys <- keys[order(keys$blq != "none", keys$n_per_time), ]
  out <- data.frame()
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(keys))) {
    current <- merge(b, keys[i, ])
    value_of <- current[match(c("percentile", "boot_se", "yuan", "delta"), current$method), ]
    boot_t <-
      sim_rows(
        comparisons$profile_summary,
        list(interval = "pknca boot-t", parameter = parameter, blq = keys$blq[i], n_per_time = keys$n_per_time[i])
      )
    out <-
      rbind(
        out,
        data.frame(
          BLQ = keys$blq[i],
          `Animals per time` = keys$n_per_time[i],
          `Coverage percentile` = round(value_of$coverage[1], 1),
          `Coverage boot. SE` = round(value_of$coverage[2], 1),
          `Coverage Yuan` = round(value_of$coverage[3], 1),
          `Coverage delta` = round(value_of$coverage[4], 1),
          `Coverage boot-t` = round(boot_t$coverage, 1),
          `CI width percentile` = round(value_of$median_ci_width[1]),
          `CI width delta` = round(value_of$median_ci_width[4]),
          `Bias (%)` = round(value_of$median_bias[1], 1),
          check.names = FALSE
        )
      )
  }
  knitr::kable(out, row.names = FALSE)
}
```

```{r simulation-bootstrap-n-auc, echo = FALSE}
show_bootstrap_n("auc")
```

```{r simulation-bootstrap-n-aumc, echo = FALSE}
show_bootstrap_n("aumc")
```

## Results:  the Tobit half-life with BLQ samples

PKNCA can also fit the half-life by Tobit regression (`hl_method = "tobit"`),
which treats BLQ samples as censored below the LLOQ rather than dropping them.
For sparse data, it fits the mean profile, with the median LLOQ of the samples
at each time and a time whose mean is BLQ censored.  With the BLQ scenarios
above (the first `r format(tobit$n_se_replicates, big.mark = ",")` data sets of
each) and the BLQ arm of the profile over the number of animals per time
(`r format(tobit$n_profile_replicates, big.mark = ",")` data sets at each
number), three estimates of $\lambda_z$ were compared:  the log-linear fit of
the mean profile ("log-linear", as above), the Tobit fit of the mean profile
("Tobit mean"), and the Tobit fit of the individual samples ("Tobit indiv.", as
the "individual" method above).  Each gave the AUC and AUMC to infinity from
the same sparse AUC to $t_{last}$ and mean at $t_{last}$, with these intervals:
Yuan's and the delta method for the log-linear fit; Yuan's for the Tobit fit
of the mean profile, which has no standard error for $\lambda_z$; Yuan's
variance plus that of $\lambda_z$ for the Tobit fit of the individual samples;
and, for each, the bootstrap percentile interval (`r tobit$n_boot` replicates,
each refitting its own $\lambda_z$).

```{r simulation-tobit, echo = FALSE}
tobit_intervals <-
  c(
    "log-linear yuan" = "Log-lin. Yuan", "log-linear delta" = "Log-lin. delta",
    "log-linear bootstrap" = "Log-lin. boot.", "tobit-mean yuan" = "Tobit mean Yuan",
    "tobit-mean bootstrap" = "Tobit mean boot.", "tobit-individual yuan+var" = "Tobit indiv. Yuan+var",
    "tobit-individual bootstrap" = "Tobit indiv. boot."
  )
tobit_methods <- c("log-linear" = "log-lin.", "tobit-mean" = "Tobit mean", "tobit-individual" = "Tobit indiv.")
# One column of `column` for each interval (or lambda.z method), in the order
# of `keys`
tobit_columns <- function(r, keys, labels, key_column, column, digits) {
  out <- list()
  for (current in names(labels)) {
    current_rows <- r[r[[key_column]] == current, ]
    # The point estimate does not depend on the interval
    current_rows <- current_rows[!duplicated(current_rows$scenario_n), ]
    out[[labels[[current]]]] <- round(current_rows[[column]][match(keys, current_rows$scenario_n)], digits)
  }
  as.data.frame(out, check.names = FALSE)
}
show_tobit <- function(parameter) {
  r <- tobit$summary[tobit$summary$parameter == parameter & tobit$summary$n_per_time == 4, ]
  r$scenario_n <- r$scenario
  first <- r[r$interval == "log-linear yuan", ]
  first <- first[order(first$scenario), ]
  coverage <- tobit_columns(r, first$scenario, tobit_intervals, "interval", "coverage", 1)
  knitr::kable(data.frame(scenario_columns(first)[, -4], coverage, check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE)
}
show_tobit_accuracy <- function(parameter) {
  r <- tobit$summary[tobit$summary$parameter == parameter & tobit$summary$n_per_time == 4, ]
  r$scenario_n <- r$scenario
  first <- r[r$interval == "log-linear yuan", ]
  first <- first[order(first$scenario), ]
  bias <- tobit_columns(r, first$scenario, tobit_methods, "lambda_z_method", "median_bias", 1)
  mae <- tobit_columns(r, first$scenario, tobit_methods, "lambda_z_method", "median_absolute_error", 1)
  names(bias) <- paste("Bias", names(bias))
  names(mae) <- paste("MAE", names(mae))
  knitr::kable(data.frame(scenario_columns(first)[, -4], bias, mae, check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE)
}
show_tobit_n <- function(parameter) {
  r <- tobit$summary[tobit$summary$parameter == parameter & tobit$summary$scenario == tobit$profile_scenario, ]
  r$scenario_n <- r$n_per_time
  keys <- sort(unique(r$n_per_time))
  coverage <- tobit_columns(r, keys, tobit_intervals, "interval", "coverage", 1)
  bias <- tobit_columns(r, keys, tobit_methods, "lambda_z_method", "median_bias", 1)
  names(bias) <- paste("Bias", names(bias))
  knitr::kable(data.frame(`Animals per time` = keys, coverage, bias, check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE)
}
```


```{r comparison-tables, echo = FALSE}
cmp <- comparisons$summary
# One column of `column` for each interval (named by `labels`), in the order
# of the scenarios `keys`
interval_columns <- function(r, keys, labels, column, digits) {
  out <- list()
  for (current in names(labels)) {
    current_rows <- r[r$interval == current, ]
    out[[labels[[current]]]] <- round(current_rows[[column]][match(keys, current_rows$scenario)], digits)
  }
  as.data.frame(out, check.names = FALSE)
}
# The rows of one interval of a summary, one per scenario, in scenario order
first_rows <- function(r, interval) {
  ret <- r[r$interval == interval, ]
  ret[order(ret$scenario), ]
}
serial_labels <-
  c(
    "pknca yuan" = "Yuan", "pknca delta" = "Delta", "pknca boot-t" = "PKNCA boot-t",
    "pk z" = "PK z", "pk boot-t" = "PK boot-t", "wj2005 z" = "WJ z", "wj2005 boot-t" = "WJ boot-t"
  )
show_serial_coverage <- function(n_per_time) {
  r <- cmp[cmp$design == "serial" & cmp$parameter == "auc" & cmp$n_per_time == n_per_time, ]
  first <- first_rows(r, "pknca delta")
  knitr::kable(
    data.frame(scenario_columns(first)[, -3], interval_columns(r, first$scenario, serial_labels, "coverage", 1), check.names = FALSE),
    row.names = FALSE
  )
}
show_serial_accuracy <- function(n_per_time) {
  r <- cmp[cmp$design == "serial" & cmp$parameter == "auc" & cmp$n_per_time == n_per_time, ]
  first <- first_rows(r, "pknca delta")
  bias <- interval_columns(r, first$scenario, c("pknca delta" = "Bias PKNCA", "pk z" = "Bias PK", "wj2005 z" = "Bias WJ"), "relative_bias", 1)
  width <-
    interval_columns(
      r, first$scenario,
      c("pknca delta" = "Width delta", "pknca boot-t" = "Width PKNCA boot-t", "pk boot-t" = "Width PK boot-t", "wj2005 boot-t" = "Width WJ boot-t"),
      "median_ci_width", 0
    )
  knitr::kable(data.frame(scenario_columns(first)[, -3], bias, width, check.names = FALSE), row.names = FALSE)
}
show_batch_coverage <- function(parameter, labels) {
  r <- cmp[cmp$design == "batch" & cmp$parameter == parameter, ]
  first <- first_rows(r, names(labels)[1])
  pk <- first_rows(r, "pk z")
  knitr::kable(
    data.frame(
      scenario_columns(first)[, -3],
      interval_columns(r, first$scenario, labels, "coverage", 1),

      check.names = FALSE

}
blq_labels <-
  c(

    "cml_impute delta" = "CML impute", "cml_direct z" = "CML direct"

# The Tobit study's values for the same scenarios (four animals per time)
tobit_auc <- tobit$summary[tobit$summary$parameter == "auc" & tobit$summary$n_per_time == 4, ]
show_blq <- function(column, tobit_column, digits) {
```
