## Results:  Wolfsegger and Jaki (2005) and the PK package

Wolfsegger and Jaki (2005) estimated the AUC to infinity in serial sacrifice
designs as the trapezoidal sum to a time $t_K$ plus $\bar{y}_K/\hat{\lambda}_z$,
with $\hat{\lambda}_z$ fit to the bias-corrected log means of the times after
$t_K$, so that the two parts are independent, and a bias correction for the
extrapolation.  They gave an asymptotic interval and a bootstrap-$t$ interval
(1000 replicates, stratified by time) on its variance, and they left open the
covariance between the trapezoidal AUC and $\hat{\lambda}_z$ when the same
samples serve both, which is what PKNCA's delta method includes.  No package
implements the 2005 estimator, so it was written from the paper ("WJ"), with
$\hat{\lambda}_z$ from the last three times as in their simulation.  The PK
package implements the later estimator of Wolfsegger and Jaki (2009) for serial
sacrifice designs and of Jaki and Wolfsegger (2012) for batch designs
(`PK::nca()`):  the trapezoidal sum to the last time plus the extrapolation
from the last mean, with $\lambda_z$ fit to the mean log concentrations of the
last `r comparisons$n_tail` times (`n.tail`), a variance that includes the
covariance of each time's mean with its mean log concentration, and asymptotic
("PK z") and bootstrap-$t$ ("PK boot-t") intervals.  PKNCA's intervals were
Yuan's, the delta method, and a bootstrap-$t$ interval on the delta-method
standard error ("PKNCA boot-t"):  the 2005 construction applied to PKNCA's
estimator, with `sparse_bootstrap()` replicates
(`r comparisons$n_boot`, each with its own half-life fit and delta-method
standard error).

All of them were run on the serial-sacrifice scenarios with three and four
animals per time (the first `r format(comparisons$n_replicates, big.mark = ",")`
data sets of each; with four animals, those of the standard error study), with
`r comparisons$pk_nsample` and `r comparisons$wj_nsample` bootstrap
replicates for PK's and WJ's bootstrap-$t$.  Both published estimators start the AUC at the first time they
are given:  for oral dosing they were given the known zero at time 0, and for
IV bolus dosing, which neither back-extrapolates, their AUC starts at the first
sample (5 minutes), which loses the area before it.  Both take the logarithm of
every sample in the tail; a BLQ sample, reported as zero, was replaced by
$10^{-256}$ in the logarithms as `PK::nca()` does, which violates their
assumption of a constant coefficient of variation in the tail.  They were run
anyway, so the BLQ scenarios show what happens when that assumption fails.

Coverage, here and below, is among the data sets for which the interval could
be calculated.  Without BLQ samples,
`r failure_range(design = "serial", blq = "none", parameter = "auc")`% of the
data sets failed, depending on the interval and scenario.  With BLQ samples, the 2005 estimator failed
(no positive $\hat{\lambda}_z$) in
`r failure_range(design = "serial", blq = "moderate", parameter = "auc", interval = "wj2005 z")`%
of them and PKNCA's estimate (no half-life) in
`r failure_range(design = "serial", blq = "moderate", parameter = "auc", interval = "pknca delta")`%.
Counting a failure as a miss would lower a coverage in the serial-sacrifice
tables by at most
`r max_coverage_drop(design = "serial", parameter = "auc")` points (the result
file has both).

Coverage (%) of the 95% intervals for the AUC to infinity with three animals
per time:

```{r comparison-serial-3, echo = FALSE}
show_serial_coverage(3)
```

And with four animals per time (the data sets of the standard error study):

```{r comparison-serial-4, echo = FALSE}
show_serial_coverage(4)
```

Bias of the point estimates (mean, % of the truth) and median width of the
intervals (% of the truth), with three animals per time:

```{r comparison-serial-accuracy-3, echo = FALSE}
show_serial_accuracy(3)
```

## Results:  the PK package's parameters in the batch design

The PK package also gives intervals for the AUMC to infinity, the MRT, the
non-compartmental half-life ($\log(2)$ times the MRT, so its coverage is the
MRT's), the clearance, and $V_{ss}$, and its help warns that the standard
errors of the MRT and $V_{ss}$ in batch designs under-cover severely.  PKNCA
gives standard errors only for the AUC and AUMC; for other parameters it has
the bootstrap.  On the batch scenarios (four animals per batch, the first
`r format(comparisons$n_replicates, big.mark = ",")` data sets of each), PK's
intervals were compared with PKNCA's delta method and bootstrap-$t$ (AUC and
AUMC) and its percentile bootstrap (MRT, the ratio of the AUMC and AUC to
infinity of each replicate).  The true MRT is that of the population mean
curve, the ratio of its AUMC and AUC; after oral dosing, it includes the mean
absorption time, as both packages' estimates do.  In a batch design,
`PK::nca()` cannot take a zero at a time where other samples are positive:
after oral dosing it stops with an error, and after IV bolus dosing it replaces
the resulting NaN variances with a placeholder ($10^{-8}$), which gives a
standard error near zero.  So every batch data set with BLQ samples was given
to PK with them omitted, as it allows (the last column gives how often), and any
interval whose standard error was PK's placeholder counted as a failure.  PK's bootstrap resamples the concentrations at each time
without regard to animal, while `sparse_bootstrap()` resamples whole animals
within each batch.

Coverage (%) for the AUC to infinity:

```{r comparison-batch-auc, echo = FALSE}
show_batch_coverage("auc", c("pknca delta" = "Delta", "pknca boot-t" = "PKNCA boot-t", "pk z" = "PK z", "pk boot-t" = "PK boot-t"))
```

For the AUMC to infinity:

```{r comparison-batch-aumc, echo = FALSE}
show_batch_coverage("aumc", c("pknca delta" = "Delta", "pknca boot-t" = "PKNCA boot-t", "pk z" = "PK z", "pk boot-t" = "PK boot-t"))
```

For the MRT, which has no analytical standard error in PKNCA:

```{r comparison-batch-mrt, echo = FALSE}
show_batch_coverage("mrt", c("pknca percentile" = "PKNCA percentile", "pk z" = "PK z", "pk boot-t" = "PK boot-t"))
```

## Results:  treatments of BLQ samples

Barnett, Geys, Jacobs, and Jaki (2021) compared eight treatments of BLQ
samples in the AUC to the last time and recommended kernel-density imputation.
Their simulations used complete designs only (10 subjects sampled at each of
six times); they noted that the methods extend to sparse designs, with the
imputed values assigned to animals at random in serial designs and by the
animals' previous concentrations in batch designs.  Their BLOQ package takes a
subject-by-time matrix, so its per-time methods were applied to the samples at
each time of each data set, and the imputed data went through PKNCA's sparse
AUC to infinity with the delta method:  zero (PKNCA's default), half the LLOQ,
regression on order statistics on the log scale (ROS), kernel-density
imputation, and censored maximum likelihood at each time followed by
imputation of the expected order statistics ("CML impute", their two-step
method).  Their direct method ("CML direct") instead uses each time's censored
maximum-likelihood mean and its variance; here those means gave the AUC to
infinity and its delta-method variance with the times independent, which the
batch design violates, and a normal interval.  The likelihood methods used
BLOQ's additive (normal) model:  its multiplicative model fits base-10
logarithms but back-transforms with the natural exponential, which does not
return the fitted mean.  As BLOQ does, a time whose samples were all BLQ took
half the LLOQ; ROS and the likelihood methods, which need two measured
samples, did the same with fewer.  Their full-likelihood method needs the
within-animal covariance of every pair of times, which one sample per animal
cannot give, so it was not run.  The scenarios are those with BLQ samples
(`r format(blq$n_replicates, big.mark = ",")` data sets each, the first of the
standard error study).  The last two columns come from the Tobit study on the
same data sets (and, for the profile's scenario, the next
`r format(tobit$n_profile_replicates - blq$n_replicates, big.mark = ",")`):
Yuan's interval with the Tobit half-life of the mean profile, and Yuan's
variance plus that of the individual-sample Tobit $\lambda_z$.

Coverage (%) of the 95% intervals for the AUC to infinity:

```{r blq-coverage, echo = FALSE}
show_blq("coverage", "coverage", 1)
```

Median bias (% of the truth):

```{r blq-bias, echo = FALSE}
show_blq("median_bias", "median_bias", 1)
```


## Findings

**Coverage of the AUC to infinity.**  With fast elimination, when
`r se_range("percent_extrapolated", parameter = "auc", method = "yuan", elimination = "fast")`%
of the AUC was extrapolated, all three methods covered close to the nominal 95%
(Yuan `r se_range("coverage", method = "yuan", parameter = "auc", elimination = "fast", digits = 1)`%,
delta `r se_range("coverage", method = "delta", parameter = "auc", elimination = "fast", digits = 1)`%,
individual `r se_range("coverage", method = "individual", parameter = "auc", elimination = "fast", digits = 1)`%),
so the uncertainty of $\lambda_z$ matters little when little is extrapolated.
With slow elimination, when
`r se_range("percent_extrapolated", parameter = "auc", method = "yuan", elimination = "slow")`%
was extrapolated, treating $\lambda_z$ as known under-covered (Yuan
`r se_range("coverage", method = "yuan", parameter = "auc", elimination = "slow", digits = 1)`%),
and the delta method was closest to nominal in every scenario
(`r se_range("coverage", method = "delta", parameter = "auc", elimination = "slow", digits = 1)`%),
though still a few points short.  Adding the variance of $\lambda_z$ from the
individual samples
(`r se_range("coverage", method = "individual", parameter = "auc", elimination = "slow", digits = 1)`%)
recovered only part of the shortfall, because it omits the covariance of
$\hat{\lambda}_z$ with the means.  The results were alike for the oral and IV
bolus routes, so back-extrapolating $C_0$ added little uncertainty, and alike
for the one- and two-compartment models and the two designs.

**Accuracy of the AUC to infinity.**  The bias of the AUC to infinity was
`r se_range("relative_bias", method = "yuan", parameter = "auc", digits = 1)`%:
slightly high with fast elimination, where the linear trapezoidal rule
overestimates the area under the declining curve, and near zero with slow
elimination (slightly low with two compartments and BLQ samples).  The median absolute errors
were similar for the two estimates of $\lambda_z$, but the log-mean
$\lambda_z$ occasionally came out near zero with slow elimination and BLQ
samples, which made the AUC to infinity heavy-tailed (RMSE up to
`r round(max(sim_rows(results, list(method = "yuan", parameter = "auc"))$rmse))`%).
The Tobit fit uses every terminal sample, including the censored ones, rather
than means that count BLQ samples as zero, and it was steadier (RMSE up to
`r round(max(sim_rows(results, list(method = "individual", parameter = "auc"))$rmse))`%).

**The AUMC to infinity.**  All three methods under-covered the AUMC in every
scenario (delta `r se_range("coverage", method = "delta", parameter = "aumc")`%,
Yuan `r se_range("coverage", method = "yuan", parameter = "aumc")`%, individual
`r se_range("coverage", method = "individual", parameter = "aumc")`%), most
with slow elimination.  Its extrapolation is proportional to $1/\lambda_z^2$,
so the first-order delta method is a poorer approximation, and the estimate is
more heavy-tailed:  its median absolute error was
`r se_range("median_absolute_error", method = "yuan", parameter = "aumc")`%,
and with two compartments and slow elimination it was biased low
(`r se_range("relative_bias", method = "yuan", parameter = "aumc", compartments = 2, elimination = "slow")`%),
because the arithmetic mean of animals with different elimination rates
declines ever more slowly, which a single exponential from $t_{last}$ misses.

**Interval width.**  The delta-method intervals were wider than Yuan's, most
when elimination was slow; the extra width is what improved the coverage.

**The bootstrap.**  With three or four animals at each time, the bootstrap
intervals were too narrow.  For the AUC to infinity, the percentile interval
covered
`r boot_range("coverage_percentile", parameter = "auc", elimination = "fast", digits = 1)`%
with fast elimination and
`r boot_range("coverage_percentile", parameter = "auc", elimination = "slow", digits = 1)`%
with slow elimination, against
`r se_range("coverage", method = "delta", parameter = "auc", elimination = "fast", digits = 1)`%
and
`r se_range("coverage", method = "delta", parameter = "auc", elimination = "slow", digits = 1)`%
for the delta method, and the interval from the bootstrap standard error was
little better
(`r boot_range("coverage_normal", parameter = "auc", digits = 1)`%).
Resampling $n$ animals understates the variance of their mean by the factor
$(n - 1)/n$ (3/4 with four animals), and the percentile interval of a skewed
estimate is narrow as well.  For the AUMC to infinity, the bootstrap covered
`r boot_range("coverage_percentile", parameter = "aumc", digits = 1)`%:  better
than Yuan's method when elimination was slow, and as good as or better than
the delta method only with slow elimination and BLQ samples, where the
first-order delta method is weakest.  The bootstrap's advantage is that it
applies to every parameter and to ratios between groups (Shen and Machado
2017), including parameters with no analytical standard error, such as Cmax and
the half-life; with few animals at each time, its intervals should be read as
too narrow.

**More animals at each time.**  The bootstrap improved with more animals, as
its $(n - 1)/n$ shortfall shrank.  Without BLQ samples, its percentile interval
for the AUC to infinity covered
`r profile_value("coverage", 4, "none", "percentile", "auc")`% with 4 animals
per time and `r profile_value("coverage", 20, "none", "percentile", "auc")`%
with 20, when the delta method covered
`r profile_value("coverage", 20, "none", "delta", "auc")`%; with BLQ samples, it
matched or passed the delta method from 6 animals per time.  Its standard
error was then as accurate as the delta method's.  But with many animals,
every interval under-covered:  with 100 animals per time, the percentile
interval covered
`r profile_value("coverage", 100, "none", "percentile", "auc")`% without and
`r profile_value("coverage", 100, "moderate", "percentile", "auc")`% with BLQ
samples (the delta method,
`r profile_value("coverage", 100, "none", "delta", "auc")`% and
`r profile_value("coverage", 100, "moderate", "delta", "auc")`%).  The cause is
the estimate, not its standard error:  the sparse AUC to infinity was biased by
`r profile_value("median_bias", 100, "none", "yuan", "auc")`% without and
`r profile_value("median_bias", 100, "moderate", "yuan", "auc")`% with BLQ
samples, whatever the number of animals, from the BLQ samples counted as zero
in the late means and the extrapolation of a mean of animals with different
elimination rates.  More animals make every interval narrower around the same
biased estimate, so no choice of interval corrects it.  The AUMC to infinity,
biased by
`r profile_value("median_bias", 100, "none", "yuan", "aumc")`% and
`r profile_value("median_bias", 100, "moderate", "yuan", "aumc")`%, showed the
same pattern sooner.

**The Tobit half-life.**  With BLQ samples, the Tobit fit of the mean profile
changed little:  the bias of the AUC to infinity was
`r tobit_range("median_bias", lambda_z_method = "tobit-mean", parameter = "auc", interval = "tobit-mean yuan", n_per_time = 4, digits = 1)`%,
against
`r tobit_range("median_bias", lambda_z_method = "log-linear", parameter = "auc", interval = "log-linear yuan", n_per_time = 4, digits = 1)`%
for the log-linear fit, and Yuan's intervals covered the same.  Its bootstrap
intervals were narrower than the log-linear fit's and covered less
(`r tobit_range("coverage", interval = "tobit-mean bootstrap", parameter = "auc", elimination = "slow", n_per_time = 4)`%
against
`r tobit_range("coverage", interval = "log-linear bootstrap", parameter = "auc", elimination = "slow", n_per_time = 4)`%
with slow elimination), and with no standard error for $\lambda_z$ it cannot use
the delta method.  The Tobit fit of the individual samples was slightly less
biased and more precise:  with 100 animals per time, its AUC to infinity was
biased by
`r tobit_value("median_bias", scenario = tobit$profile_scenario, n_per_time = 100, interval = "tobit-individual yuan+var", parameter = "auc")`%
and its AUMC by
`r tobit_value("median_bias", scenario = tobit$profile_scenario, n_per_time = 100, interval = "tobit-individual yuan+var", parameter = "aumc")`%,
against
`r tobit_value("median_bias", scenario = tobit$profile_scenario, n_per_time = 100, interval = "log-linear yuan", parameter = "auc")`%
and
`r tobit_value("median_bias", scenario = tobit$profile_scenario, n_per_time = 100, interval = "log-linear yuan", parameter = "aumc")`%
for the log-linear fit.  Its intervals were still less reliable than the delta
method with few animals per time, and with many animals the bias left every
interval short of nominal, whichever $\lambda_z$ was used.  So most of the
bias that BLQ samples add does not come from $\lambda_z$, and a better fit of
$\lambda_z$ does not remove it:  it comes from the late means, where BLQ
samples count as zero, and from the mean profile ending earlier, when more
than half of a time's samples are BLQ.

**Published estimators with three or four animals per time.**  Without BLQ
samples, no interval was best everywhere.  With three animals per time, the
delta method covered
`r serial_range("coverage", "pknca delta", 3, blq = "none")`%, PKNCA's
bootstrap-$t$ `r serial_range("coverage", "pknca boot-t", 3, blq = "none")`%,
PK's asymptotic and bootstrap-$t$ intervals
`r serial_range("coverage", "pk z", 3, blq = "none")`% and
`r serial_range("coverage", "pk boot-t", 3, blq = "none")`%, and the 2005
estimator's `r serial_range("coverage", "wj2005 z", 3, blq = "none")`% and
`r serial_range("coverage", "wj2005 boot-t", 3, blq = "none")`%.  With slow
elimination, the 2005 bootstrap-$t$ came closest to nominal
(`r serial_range("coverage", "wj2005 boot-t", 3, blq = "none", elimination = "slow")`%,
against
`r serial_range("coverage", "pknca delta", 3, blq = "none", elimination = "slow")`%
for the delta method), and it covered better than their asymptotic interval, as
Wolfsegger and Jaki found.  But it was about twice as wide (median
`r serial_range("median_ci_width", "wj2005 boot-t", 3, blq = "none", elimination = "slow", digits = 0)`%
of the truth, against
`r serial_range("median_ci_width", "pknca delta", 3, blq = "none", elimination = "slow", digits = 0)`%),
because its estimate was unstable:  its median bias was
`r serial_range("median_bias", "wj2005 z", 3, blq = "none")`%, against
`r serial_range("median_bias", "pknca delta", 3, blq = "none")`% for PKNCA's
estimate and `r serial_range("median_bias", "pk z", 3, blq = "none")`% for PK's.
With `r format(comparisons$large_n_per_time, big.mark = ",")` animals per time
(`r comparisons$n_large_replicates` data sets of each scenario without BLQ
samples), the 2005 estimate was biased by
`r large_range("wj2005", elimination = "fast")`% with fast elimination, much as
PKNCA's was (`r large_range("pknca", elimination = "fast")`%), from the linear
trapezoidal rule over a declining curve, and by
`r large_range("wj2005", elimination = "slow")`% with slow elimination
(PKNCA's, `r large_range("pknca", elimination = "slow")`%).  So its large
errors with three or four animals are those of small samples:
its bias correction divides the variance of $\hat{\lambda}_z$ by
$\hat{\lambda}_z^3$, its correction of the log means divides one noisy variance
by a noisy squared mean, and the variability of the elimination rate here gives
the late times a coefficient of variation far above the 5% to 20% of their
simulation.  Its construction also extrapolates from $t_K$, three times before
the last, rather than from $t_{last}$, so more of the AUC rests on
$\hat{\lambda}_z$.  That is the price of keeping $\hat{\lambda}_z$ independent
of the trapezoidal sum; the delta method instead keeps every time in the sum
and includes the covariance that Wolfsegger and Jaki (2005) left open.

With BLQ samples, the published estimators broke down:  a zero among the
logarithms (taken as $10^{-256}$) drags the mean log concentration of the last
time down and $\hat{\lambda}_z$ up.  The 2005 estimator's intervals covered
`r serial_range("coverage", "wj2005 boot-t", 3, blq = "moderate", digits = 0)`%
in every scenario with BLQ samples.  PK's intervals held up with fast elimination
(`r serial_range("coverage", "pk z", 3, blq = "moderate", elimination = "fast")`%,
asymptotic), where little is extrapolated, but covered
`r serial_range("coverage", "pk z", 3, blq = "moderate", elimination = "slow", digits = 0)`%
(asymptotic) and
`r serial_range("coverage", "pk boot-t", 3, blq = "moderate", elimination = "slow", digits = 0)`%
(bootstrap-$t$) with slow elimination, while the delta method covered
`r serial_range("coverage", "pknca delta", 3, blq = "moderate")`% with BLQ
samples.  Over every
serial-sacrifice scenario with three animals per time, the delta method covered
best, `r serial_range("coverage", "pknca delta", 3)`%, against
`r serial_range("coverage", "pknca boot-t", 3)`% for PKNCA's bootstrap-$t$,
`r serial_range("coverage", "pk boot-t", 3)`% for PK's, and
`r serial_range("coverage", "wj2005 boot-t", 3)`% for the 2005 estimator's;
with four animals per time, the delta method covered
`r serial_range("coverage", "pknca delta", 4)`%.

**The PK package in the batch design.**  Without BLQ samples, PK's asymptotic
interval for the AUC to infinity covered
`r batch_range("coverage", "pk z", "auc", blq = "none")`% and its bootstrap-$t$
`r batch_range("coverage", "pk boot-t", "auc", blq = "none")`%, against
`r batch_range("coverage", "pknca delta", "auc", blq = "none")`% for the delta
method and `r batch_range("coverage", "pknca boot-t", "auc", blq = "none")`%
for PKNCA's bootstrap-$t$.  PK's bootstrap-$t$ resamples the concentrations at
each time without regard to the animal they came from, although each animal
gives several samples, and it under-covered every parameter.  For the AUMC to infinity, PK's intervals
covered `r batch_range("coverage", "pk z", "aumc", blq = "none")`% (asymptotic)
and `r batch_range("coverage", "pk boot-t", "aumc", blq = "none")`%
(bootstrap-$t$), against
`r batch_range("coverage", "pknca delta", "aumc", blq = "none")`% for the delta
method and `r batch_range("coverage", "pknca boot-t", "aumc", blq = "none")`%
for PKNCA's bootstrap-$t$.  The under-coverage that PK's help warns of for the
MRT and $V_{ss}$ was confirmed:  the asymptotic intervals covered
`r batch_range("coverage", "pk z", "mrt", blq = "none")`% for the MRT (and so
for the non-compartmental half-life) and
`r batch_range("coverage", "pk z", "vss", route = "iv", blq = "none")`% for
$V_{ss}$ after an IV bolus, while the clearance, a function of the AUC alone,
covered `r batch_range("coverage", "pk z", "cl", blq = "none")`%.  The cause is
mostly the estimate rather than its standard error:  the MRT of the mean
profile was biased by
`r batch_range("median_bias", "pk z", "mrt", blq = "none")`% (PK) and
`r batch_range("median_bias", "pknca percentile", "mrt", blq = "none")`%
(PKNCA), because the AUMC to infinity is underestimated, and PKNCA's percentile
bootstrap of the MRT covered no better
(`r batch_range("coverage", "pknca percentile", "mrt", blq = "none")`%).  With
BLQ samples, every batch data set that had any
(`r batch_range("percent_fallback", "pk z", "auc", blq = "moderate", digits = 0)`%
of each scenario) went to PK with them omitted.  Dropping the lowest late
concentrations biased PK's AUC to infinity high (median
`r batch_range("median_bias", "pk z", "auc", blq = "moderate")`%), but its
asymptotic interval still covered
`r batch_range("coverage", "pk z", "auc", blq = "moderate")`%, against
`r batch_range("coverage", "pknca delta", "auc", blq = "moderate")`% for the
delta method.

**PKNCA's bootstrap-$t$.**  The bootstrap-$t$ on the delta-method standard
error covered about as well as the delta method without BLQ samples, but less
well with BLQ samples and slow elimination
(`r serial_range("coverage", "pknca boot-t", 3, blq = "moderate", elimination = "slow")`%
against
`r serial_range("coverage", "pknca delta", 3, blq = "moderate", elimination = "slow")`%
with three animals per time), and its intervals were wider.  Over the number of
animals per time (the first
`r format(comparisons$n_profile_replicates, big.mark = ",")` data sets of each),
it matched the delta method for the AUC to infinity without BLQ samples
(`r boott_value("coverage", 4, "none", "auc")`% and
`r boott_value("coverage", 100, "none", "auc")`% with 4 and 100 animals, against
`r boott_value("coverage", 4, "none", "auc", interval = "pknca delta")`% and
`r boott_value("coverage", 100, "none", "auc", interval = "pknca delta")`%), and
it covered the AUMC to infinity better
(`r boott_value("coverage", 4, "none", "aumc")`% and
`r boott_value("coverage", 100, "none", "aumc")`%, against
`r boott_value("coverage", 4, "none", "aumc", interval = "pknca delta")`% and
`r boott_value("coverage", 100, "none", "aumc", interval = "pknca delta")`%).
But it keeps the same point estimate, and so the same bias:  the AUMC to
infinity was biased by
`r boott_value("median_bias", 4, "none", "aumc", interval = "pknca delta")`%
with 4 animals and
`r boott_value("median_bias", 100, "none", "aumc", interval = "pknca delta")`%
with 100 in both rows.  Its better coverage comes from the interval, not from
a better estimate.  With 4 animals per time it was
`r boott_width_ratio(4, "none", "aumc")` times as wide as the delta method's;
with 100 it was about as wide
(`r boott_width_ratio(100, "none", "aumc")` times), but its asymmetric
quantiles moved it up toward the truth, so the share of intervals entirely
below the truth fell from
`r boott_value("miss_low", 100, "none", "aumc", interval = "pknca delta")`% to
`r boott_value("miss_low", 100, "none", "aumc")`%.  An interval that widens or
moves around a biased estimate is not a better method for it, so the
bootstrap-$t$ is not adopted; the bias of the estimate, which limits every
interval with many animals, is the thing to reduce.

**Treatments of BLQ samples.**  With fast elimination, the treatment hardly
mattered:  every imputation covered
`r blq_range("coverage", elimination = "fast", interval = c("half_lloq delta", "ros delta", "kernel delta", "cml_impute delta"), digits = 1)`%,
as zero substitution did
(`r blq_range("coverage", elimination = "fast", interval = "zero delta", digits = 1)`%).
With slow elimination, imputing the BLQ samples reduced the bias of zero
substitution (median
`r blq_range("median_bias", elimination = "slow", interval = "zero delta", digits = 1)`%):
ROS most
(`r blq_range("median_bias", elimination = "slow", interval = "ros delta", digits = 1)`%),
then kernel imputation
(`r blq_range("median_bias", elimination = "slow", interval = "kernel delta", digits = 1)`%),
half the LLOQ
(`r blq_range("median_bias", elimination = "slow", interval = "half_lloq delta", digits = 1)`%),
and the censored likelihood
(`r blq_range("median_bias", elimination = "slow", interval = "cml_impute delta", digits = 1)`%).
But the imputed values also narrowed the intervals, so coverage fell by a few
points (zero
`r blq_range("coverage", elimination = "slow", interval = "zero delta", digits = 1)`%,
kernel
`r blq_range("coverage", elimination = "slow", interval = "kernel delta", digits = 1)`%,
ROS
`r blq_range("coverage", elimination = "slow", interval = "ros delta", digits = 1)`%).
The direct method under-covered
(`r blq_range("coverage", interval = "cml_direct z", digits = 1)`%), most in
the batch design
(`r blq_range("coverage", interval = "cml_direct z", design = "batch", digits = 1)`%),
whose correlation between times it ignores, as Barnett et al. found with
correlated samples in complete designs.  The additive two-step method imputed a
negative concentration in
`r summary_range(blq$fallbacks, "percent_with_negative", interval = "cml_impute delta")`%
of the data sets.  ROS and the likelihood methods fell back to half the LLOQ at
some time in
`r summary_range(blq$fallbacks, "percent_with_fallback", interval = "ros delta")`%
of the data sets, because a time had fewer than two measured samples; kernel
imputation, which needs one, fell back in
`r summary_range(blq$fallbacks, "percent_with_fallback", interval = "kernel delta", digits = 1)`%.
For the AUC to the last time in complete designs, Barnett et al. recommended
kernel imputation; for the sparse AUC to infinity here, it removed about half
of the bias with slow elimination at the cost of a point or two of coverage.
None of the treatments gave both less bias and better coverage than zero
substitution, and neither did the Tobit half-life.

# Arithmetic or geometric mean profiles

The sparse AUC uses the arithmetic mean at each time, whose profile is the
population mean concentration curve.  A geometric mean profile instead
approximates the typical animal, and it may be less affected by animals with
high concentrations.  The second study compared the two for the AUClast,
AUCinf, Cmax ($C_0$ for IV bolus), AUMClast, AUMCinf, and half-life, using the
same design with `r format(mean_type$n_replicates, big.mark = ",")` replicates
per scenario.

For each replicate, both mean profiles were formed, and `pk.nca()` calculated
the parameters from each with the linear trapezoidal rule (imputing zero at
time 0 for oral dosing and back-extrapolating $C_0$ for IV bolus).  For the
geometric mean, a time with more than half of its samples BLQ was BLQ (as for
the arithmetic sparse mean), and otherwise BLQ samples counted as half of the
LLOQ.  Each profile was compared with its own target (the arithmetic or
geometric mean of the individual parameters of
`r format(mean_type$n_virtual, big.mark = ",")` virtual animals) and with the
typical animal.  Precision is the robust coefficient of variation (the
interquartile range divided by 1.349, relative to the median).

```{r mean-type-summary, echo = FALSE}
mt <- mean_type$summary
parameter_labels <-
  c(auclast = "AUClast", aucinf = "AUCinf", cmax = "Cmax (C0 for IV)",
    aumclast = "AUMClast", aumcinf = "AUMCinf", half.life = "Half-life")
range_text <- function(x) paste(round(range(x)), collapse = " to ")
out <- data.frame()
for (current_parameter in names(parameter_labels)) {
  a <- mt[mt$parameter == current_parameter & mt$mean_type == "arithmetic", ]
  g <- mt[mt$parameter == current_parameter & mt$mean_type == "geometric", ]
  g <- g[match(a$scenario, g$scenario), ]
  out <-
    rbind(
      out,
      data.frame(
        Parameter = parameter_labels[[current_parameter]],
        `Bias vs own target, arith.` = range_text(a$bias_natural),
        `Bias vs own target, geom.` = range_text(g$bias_natural),
        `Bias vs typical, arith.` = range_text(a$bias_typical),
        `Bias vs typical, geom.` = range_text(g$bias_typical),
        `Robust CV, arith.` = range_text(a$robust_cv),
        `Robust CV, geom.` = range_text(g$robust_cv),
        `Geom. CV lower (scenarios)` = sprintf("%d of %d", sum(g$robust_cv < a$robust_cv - 1), nrow(a)),
        check.names = FALSE
      )
    )
}
knitr::kable(out, row.names = FALSE, caption = "Bias (median, %) and robust CV (%) over the scenarios; the last column counts the scenarios where the geometric robust CV was more than 1 point lower.")
```

```{r mean-type-half-life, echo = FALSE}
hl <- mt[mt$parameter == "half.life", ]
keys <- unique(hl[, c("compartments", "elimination", "blq")])
keys <- keys[order(keys$compartments, keys$elimination, keys$blq), ]
out_hl <- data.frame()
for (i in seq_len(nrow(keys))) {
  current <- merge(hl, keys[i, ])
  out_hl <-
    rbind(
      out_hl,
      data.frame(
        Model = paste0(keys$compartments[i], "-cmt"),
        Elimination = keys$elimination[i],
        BLQ = keys$blq[i],
        `Arithmetic` = range_text(current$bias_typical[current$mean_type == "arithmetic"]),
        `Geometric` = range_text(current$bias_typical[current$mean_type == "geometric"]),
        check.names = FALSE
      )
    )
}
knitr::kable(out_hl, row.names = FALSE, caption = "Bias (%) of the half-life of the mean profile against the typical animal's half-life, over routes and designs.")
```

**Findings.**  Against their own targets, the two profiles were similarly
accurate for the AUCs and Cmax.  The geometric profile was as precise or more
precise, most clearly for the half-life with BLQ samples and for the AUMC to
infinity, but the gains were modest elsewhere.  Both underestimated the AUMC to
infinity (arithmetic
`r mt_range("bias_natural", mean_type = "arithmetic", parameter = "aumcinf")`%,
geometric `r mt_range("bias_natural", mean_type = "geometric", parameter = "aumcinf")`%).
The half-life of the arithmetic mean profile was not consistently too short:
it was too long when the terminal phase was well sampled, because the late mean
is dominated by the slowly eliminating animals, and too short with BLQ samples
(counted as zero in the late means) and in the two-compartment model with slow
elimination, where the fitted points reach back toward the distribution phase.
The geometric profile was generally a few percent short, because the
geometric mean of exponentials declines at the average elimination rate.

The geometric profile was not adopted.  Its gains were modest; it estimates a
different quantity (the typical animal rather than the population mean curve);
its BLQ rule (here, half the LLOQ) is a choice that drives its results with BLQ
samples; and the sparse variance methods (Bailer, Nedelman and Jia, Holder)
are for arithmetic means, so adopting it would change every sparse calculation.

# Calculating it with PKNCA

Request `aucinf.obs` (or `aumcinf.obs`) with sparse data.  The standard error
and degrees of freedom are reported with it as `aucinf.obs_se` and
`aucinf.obs_df`, and the summary shows the estimate with its standard error.
These animals were not sampled at the dose, so the concentration at time 0 is
imputed as zero.

```{r pknca-example}
d_sparse <-
  data.frame(
    time = rep(c(0.5, 1, 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, 24), each = 4),
    conc =
      c(3.1, 4.4, 3.6, 5.2,  5.8, 6.9, 5.1, 7.4,  7.2, 6.1, 8.3, 6.6,
        5.0, 6.2, 4.4, 5.6,  4.1, 3.4, 4.8, 3.7,  2.9, 3.5, 2.4, 3.1,
        1.6, 1.9, 1.3, 1.8,  0.33, 0.27, 0.41, 0.30)
  )
d_sparse$animal <- seq_len(nrow(d_sparse))
o_data <-
  PKNCAdata(
    PKNCAconc(d_sparse, conc ~ time | animal, sparse = TRUE),
    intervals = data.frame(start = 0, end = Inf, aucinf.obs = TRUE, aumcinf.obs = TRUE),
    impute = "start_conc0"
  )
o_nca <- pk.nca(o_data)
d_result <- as.data.frame(o_nca)
d_result[grepl("^au.*inf|^lambda.z$", d_result$PPTESTCD), c("PPTESTCD", "PPORRES")]
summary(o_nca)
```

The `sparse_lambda_z_se` option (set globally with `PKNCA.options()` or for
one analysis with the `options` argument of `PKNCAdata()`) is `"delta"` (the
default) for the delta method or `"none"` for Yuan's method.  The method used
is recorded in the `PPANMETH` column.

After an IV bolus, request the IV parameters; $C_0$ is back-extrapolated from
the mean profile, and no imputation is needed.

```{r pknca-example-iv}
d_sparse_iv <-
  data.frame(
    time = rep(c(0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8, 24), each = 4),
    conc =
      c(9.1, 10.4, 8.7, 9.9,  8.8, 9.5, 8.1, 9.2,  8.2, 7.6, 8.9, 7.9,
        6.4, 7.1, 6.0, 6.9,  4.6, 4.1, 5.0, 4.3,  2.1, 1.8, 2.3, 1.9,
        0.10, 0.08, 0.12, 0.09)
  )
d_sparse_iv$animal <- seq_len(nrow(d_sparse_iv))
o_data_iv <-
  PKNCAdata(
    PKNCAconc(d_sparse_iv, conc ~ time | animal, sparse = TRUE),
    PKNCAdose(data.frame(time = 0, dose = 100), dose ~ time, route = "intravascular"),
    intervals = data.frame(start = 0, end = Inf, c0 = TRUE, aucivinf.obs = TRUE)
  )
d_result_iv <- as.data.frame(suppressWarnings(pk.nca(o_data_iv)))
d_result_iv[grepl("^c0$|^aucivinf", d_result_iv$PPTESTCD), c("PPTESTCD", "PPORRES")]
```

The warnings suppressed here say that the AUCs from time 0 without $C_0$
(`aucinf.obs`, which `aucivinf.obs` depends on) are not calculated.

# Discussion

When $\lambda_z$ is estimated from the same samples, its uncertainty adds to
that of the AUC to infinity, and treating it as known, as Yuan's (1993)
standard error does, under-covers once the extrapolated area is a substantial
part of the AUC.  The delta method on the log means is a consistent extension of
Yuan's method:  it keeps his estimate, applies to serial-sacrifice and batch
designs alike through the covariance of the means, includes the covariance of
$\hat{\lambda}_z$ with $C_{last}$ and the AUC to $t_{last}$, and needs nothing
beyond the quantities already used for the sparse AUC to $t_{last}$.  In the
simulation it brought the coverage of the AUC to infinity much closer to
nominal when the extrapolated area was large
(`r se_range("coverage", method = "delta", parameter = "auc", elimination = "slow", digits = 1)`%,
against `r se_range("coverage", method = "yuan", parameter = "auc", elimination = "slow", digits = 1)`%
for Yuan), though still a few points short, and it cost little when the
extrapolated area was small.  For this reason, it is PKNCA's default
(`sparse_lambda_z_se = "delta"`).  The same delta method carries the
uncertainty of the back-extrapolated $C_0$ after an IV bolus, and the IV bolus
scenarios covered as well as the oral ones.

Estimating $\lambda_z$ from the individual samples with a (mixed-effects) Tobit
regression gave a more stable point estimate when samples were BLQ, but adding
its variance to Yuan's did not give adequate coverage, and its mixed-effects
fit was itself occasionally unstable in the batch design with BLQ samples and
slow elimination.  A bootstrap over animals, which includes the covariance of
that $\lambda_z$ with the means, was too narrow with few animals per time, as
every bootstrap was.  The Tobit fit of the mean profile, which uses the LLOQs,
gave nearly the same results as the log-linear fit.  Neither Tobit fit removed
the bias of the sparse estimate with BLQ samples, which comes mostly from
counting BLQ samples as zero in the late means and from the mean profile
ending earlier.  Estimating those means with the censoring taken into account,
by the imputations and censored likelihoods that Barnett et al. (2021)
compared, removed part of that bias with slow elimination, but the imputed
values also narrowed the intervals, so none covered better than zero
substitution, and the direct censored likelihood, which treats the times as
independent, under-covered.

Against the published estimators for these designs, the delta method held up
best with three or four animals per time.  The estimator of Wolfsegger and
Jaki (2005) avoids the covariance of $\hat{\lambda}_z$ with the trapezoidal sum
by fitting $\hat{\lambda}_z$ only after it; with few animals, its bias
corrections made it unstable and its bootstrap-$t$ intervals about twice as
wide.  The estimators of the PK package include the covariance of each time's
mean with its mean log concentration and covered a few points less than the
delta method without BLQ samples.  Neither published estimator has a rule for
BLQ samples:  the 2005 estimator broke down with any BLQ samples, and PK's with
BLQ samples and slow elimination, where PKNCA's rule of ending the mean profile
at a time with more than half of its samples BLQ kept the delta method near
nominal.  In the batch design, PK's bootstrap-$t$, which resamples
concentrations rather than animals, under-covered every parameter, and its MRT
and $V_{ss}$ intervals under-covered as its help warns, mostly because the MRT
of the mean profile is itself biased.

Limitations remain.  The delta method conditions on the selected half-life
points, so the uncertainty of the automatic point selection is not included; it
is a first-order approximation, which is least accurate when $\lambda_z$ is
imprecise, as for the AUMC with slow elimination; and the arithmetic mean
profile of animals with different elimination rates is not monoexponential, so
the extrapolation $C_{last}/\lambda_z$ is itself biased for the population mean
curve, which is part of why the AUMC to infinity is underestimated.  Where the
extrapolated area is large, sampling longer remains the better remedy.

## Extensions beyond the published methods

PKNCA has these, which the published methods compared here do not:

* **The covariance of $\hat{\lambda}_z$ with every mean, in any design.**  The
  delta method takes it from the covariance of the means (Holder's, for batch
  and complete designs), which answers the question Wolfsegger and Jaki (2005)
  left open.  Their later estimators (PK) include the covariance of each time's
  mean with its own mean log concentration.
* **The uncertainty of the back-extrapolated $C_0$** after an IV bolus.  PK and
  the 2005 estimator start the AUC at the first sample.
* **$\lambda_z$ from the log arithmetic means at PKNCA's automatic choice of
  half-life points**, the same $\lambda_z$ as the point estimate, rather than
  from the mean log concentrations of a fixed number of last times, and
  Satterthwaite degrees of freedom for $t$ intervals.
* **A rule for BLQ samples:**  a time with more than half of its samples BLQ
  ends the mean profile, and the Tobit half-life carries the LLOQ through the
  mean profile.  The published estimators take the logarithm of every sample.
* **An evaluation of arithmetic and geometric mean profiles.**
* **A stratified bootstrap of whole animals** (`sparse_bootstrap()`) for any
  parameter.

The published methods have these, which PKNCA does not adopt, for the reasons
the results give:

* **Standard errors of the MRT, clearance, $V_{ss}$, and non-compartmental
  half-life** (PK).  PKNCA gives standard errors only for the AUC and AUMC.
  PK's intervals for the MRT and $V_{ss}$ under-covered in the batch design
  (`r batch_range("coverage", "pk z", "mrt", blq = "none")`% for the MRT
  without BLQ samples), mostly from the bias of the MRT estimate, which a
  standard error cannot fix.
* **$\lambda_z$ fit after the trapezoidal sum, with a bias correction**
  (Wolfsegger and Jaki 2005):  as accurate as PKNCA's estimate with many
  animals, but unstable
  with three or four, and its intervals about twice as wide.
* **Bootstrap-$t$ intervals** (both papers):  on PKNCA's delta-method standard
  error, the bootstrap-$t$ covered the AUMC better than the delta method, but
  not the AUC, and covered the AUC worse with BLQ samples.  It keeps the same
  point estimate and so the same bias
  (`r boott_value("median_bias", 4, "none", "aumc", interval = "pknca delta")`%
  for the AUMC with 4 animals per time, in both); its gain in coverage
  (`r boott_value("coverage", 4, "none", "aumc", interval = "pknca delta")`% to
  `r boott_value("coverage", 4, "none", "aumc")`%) comes from an interval
  `r boott_width_ratio(4, "none", "aumc")` times as wide, and with many
  animals from one shifted around the same biased estimate, which is not a
  better method.
* **Imputation of BLQ samples** (Barnett et al. 2021):  ROS and kernel
  imputation reduced the bias with slow elimination, but none covered better
  than zero substitution, and each needs measured samples at the time, which
  three or four animals do not always give.
* **The full likelihood over all times** (Barnett et al. 2021), which needs the
  within-animal covariance of every pair of times and so cannot apply with one
  sample per animal.
